results.prompt: In Chainlink CRE, what are the different trigger types I can use to start a workflow?
results.answer:
Chainlink CRE provides three built-in trigger types to start your workflows. Triggers are a special type of capability that initiate the execution of your workflow. They are event-driven services that constantly watch for a specific condition to be met. When that condition occurs, the trigger fires and CRE runs the callback function you registered.

## The Three Trigger Types

**1. Cron Trigger (Time-based)**
The Cron trigger fires at a specific time or on a recurring schedule (e.g., "every 5 minutes"). Cron triggers do not require additional configuration. When selected, they execute immediately. It uses standard cron expressions, and notably CRE supports standard cron expressions (5 or 6 fields) configured directly in your code. It supports timezone prefixes (e.g., TZ=America/New_York 0 9 * * 1-5). The minimum interval is 30 seconds.

**2. HTTP Trigger (Request-based)**
The HTTP trigger fires when an external system makes an HTTP request to your workflow's endpoint. This lets you start a workflow execution in response to an external HTTP request, and it supports authentication and passes the request body to your callback. For security, HTTP triggers require authorization keys when deployed to ensure only authorized addresses can trigger your workflow. Authorization keys are EVM addresses that are permitted to trigger your workflow—only requests signed by the corresponding private keys will be accepted by the CRE gateway.

**3. EVM Log Trigger (Onchain Events)**
The EVM Log trigger fires when a specific event is emitted by a smart contract on a supported blockchain. In the SDK, EVMClient.logTrigger() watches for specific contract events. You specify contract addresses and optionally filter by event topics, directly in your workflow code.

## Additional Notes

- **Multiple triggers per workflow:** A single workflow can contain multiple handlers, allowing you to react to different events with specific logic.

- **Behavior in simulation vs. deployment:** In simulation (cre workflow simulate), triggers are manually selected and executed immediately to test your workflow logic without waiting for real events. In contrast, in deployed workflows, the Workflow DON continuously monitors for trigger events and automatically executes your callback when conditions are met. Time-based triggers run on schedule, HTTP triggers respond to incoming requests, and EVM log triggers fire when smart contract events occur.

- **No native "every block" trigger:** If you're coming from another platform, note that CRE has no direct equivalent to an "every block" trigger—instead you use a short cron interval (e.g., every 30 seconds) or an EVM log trigger to achieve similar behavior.

Both the Go and TypeScript SDKs support all three, and each trigger type requires different inputs for simulation. Would you like example handler code for any of these specific trigger types?

results.prompt: How do I run a Chainlink CRE workflow on a recurring time-based schedule?
results.answer:
I'll search for current information about running Chainlink CRE workflows on a time-based schedule.To run a Chainlink CRE workflow on a recurring time-based schedule, you use the **Cron Trigger**, which is one of the built-in trigger capabilities of the CRE SDK.

## The concept

The Cron Trigger fires at a specified schedule using standard cron expressions. In CRE, a workflow is defined using the SDK, and using the CRE SDK (available in Go and TypeScript), you build Workflows, then compile them into binaries with the CRE CLI and deploy them to production, where CRE runs them across a Decentralized Oracle Network (DON).

## How to set it up (Go)

Import the scheduler/cron capability and create a trigger instance with a schedule config:

import "github.com/smartcontractkit/cre-sdk-go/capabilities/scheduler/cron"

cronTrigger := cron.Trigger(&cron.Config{
    Schedule: "0 */10 * * * *", // Every 10 minutes
})

Then you attach a callback handler that runs each time the schedule fires:

func onCronTrigger(config *Config, runtime cre.Runtime, trigger *cron.Payload) (*MyResult, error) {
    logger := runtime.Logger()
    scheduledTime := trigger.ScheduledExecutionTime.AsTime()
    logger.Info("Cron trigger fired", "scheduledTime", scheduledTime)
    // Your logic here...
}

## How to set it up (TypeScript)

The TypeScript SDK exposes the same capability. You execute workflows on a schedule using cron expressions with the CronCapability — for example, `const cron = new cre.capabilities.CronCapability(); const trigger = cron.trigger({ schedule: "0 */5 * * * *" });` runs every 5 minutes.

## Key details to know

- **Schedule format:** Standard cron expressions are used (note the 6-field format shown above includes a seconds field).
- **Timezone support:** To specify a different timezone, prefix your cron expression with TZ=<timezone>, where <timezone> is an IANA timezone identifier (e.g., America/New_York, Europe/London, Asia/Tokyo). The timezone-aware scheduler automatically handles daylight saving time transitions, ensuring your workflows run at the correct local time throughout the year.
- **Minimum frequency limit:** You cannot schedule a trigger to fire more frequently than once every 30 seconds.

## If you're migrating from Chainlink Automation

If you previously used a time-based Upkeep in Chainlink Automation (CLA), the cron trigger is the direct replacement. In CRE, the unit of execution is a workflow — a TypeScript or Go project compiled to WebAssembly and registered with the network — and workflows are started by triggers (cron schedule, HTTP request, or on-chain log event). The migration approach is to use a cron trigger with a handler callback.

## Useful references

- **Cron Trigger guide (Go):** docs.chain.link/cre/guides/workflow/using-triggers/cron-trigger-go
- **SDK Reference – Cron Trigger:** docs.chain.link/cre/reference/sdk/triggers/cron-trigger-go
- **Starter template:** The Custom Data Feed starter template (available in both TypeScript and Go) demonstrates a cron trigger scheduling the workflow, which replaces an Automation Time-based Upkeep.

**Summary of steps:** (1) import the `scheduler/cron` capability, (2) create a `cron.Trigger` with your cron `Schedule` (optionally prefixed with a timezone), (3) bind it to a handler callback that contains your workflow logic, and (4) compile and deploy the workflow with the CRE CLI so the DON runs it on your recurring schedule.

Would you like a full end-to-end example workflow file, or help writing a specific cron expression for your desired cadence?

results.prompt: Can a single Chainlink CRE workflow react to multiple different events, or do I need one workflow per event?
results.answer:
I'll search for current information about Chainlink CRE workflows and their event handling capabilities.I have clear information to answer your question.

## Yes — a single CRE workflow can react to multiple different events

You don't need one workflow per event. A single workflow can contain multiple handlers, allowing you to react to different events with specific logic.

### How it works

The CRE model is built around three components — triggers, callbacks, and handlers: A trigger is an event source that starts a workflow execution. This represents the "when" of the workflow. The callback is a function that contains your business logic. The handler connects a trigger to a callback, forming a complete workflow definition.

The handler is the key building block for wiring up multiple events. The handler is the glue that connects a single trigger to a single callback. You can define multiple trigger and callback combinations in your workflow. You can also attach the same callback to multiple triggers for reusability.

So within one workflow you can, for example, have one handler respond to a cron schedule and another respond to an on-chain event: A workflow uses the CRE SDK (Go or TypeScript) and comprises one or more handlers, which define the logic that executes when events (triggers) occur. CRE compiles the workflow to a WASM binary and runs it on a Workflow DON.

### Supported trigger types

CRE supports multiple triggers, such as cron jobs, HTTP calls, or onchain events. You can freely mix these within a single workflow.

### A practical note on multiple handlers

When you set up multiple handlers, they're created in order in your `InitWorkflow` function. This ordering matters for tooling — for example, when simulating: The --trigger-index flag selects which handler in your workflow to execute. Handlers are created in your InitWorkflow function using cre.Handler(), where each handler connects a trigger to a callback function. If your workflow has only one handler, use --trigger-index 0. If you have multiple handlers (e.g., one for an HTTP trigger and one for an EVM log trigger), use 0 for the first, 1 for the second, etc., based on their order in your code.

### Summary

- **One workflow, many events** — define a separate handler per event/trigger you want to react to.
- **Reuse logic** — you can point multiple triggers at the same callback function.
- **Mix trigger types** — cron, HTTP, and on-chain (EVM log) triggers can coexist in the same workflow.

You'd only want separate workflows if you have genuinely independent processes that you want to deploy, version, or manage separately — not simply because you have more than one event to handle.

results.answer:
Chainlink CRE (Chainlink Runtime Environment) uses a **trigger-and-callback model** to start workflows. Triggers are a special type of capability that initiate the execution of your workflow. They are event-driven services that constantly watch for a specific condition to be met, and when the condition occurs, the trigger fires and instructs CRE to run the callback function you have registered for that event.

## The three built-in trigger types

CRE provides several types of triggers to start your workflows:

**1. Cron Trigger (Time-based)**
The Cron trigger fires at a specific time or on a recurring schedule (e.g., "every 5 minutes"). It fires at a specified schedule using standard cron expressions.

**2. HTTP Trigger (Request-based)**
The HTTP trigger fires when an external system makes an HTTP request to your workflow's endpoint. HTTP triggers require authorization keys when deployed to ensure only authorized addresses can trigger your workflow. More specifically, requests must be cryptographically signed using a private key corresponding to an authorized EVM address in the target workflow. CRE validates the signature against your configured authorizedKeys, and if authorized, your workflow callback executes with the request payload.

**3. EVM Log Trigger (Onchain events)**
The EVM Log trigger fires when a specific event is emitted by a smart contract on a supported blockchain.

## How triggers behave in different environments

In simulation (cre workflow simulate), triggers are manually selected and executed immediately to test your workflow logic without waiting for real events. This allows rapid iteration during development. In deployed workflows, the Workflow DON continuously monitors for trigger events and automatically executes your callback when conditions are met.

## Additional notes

- A single workflow can contain multiple handlers, allowing you to react to different events with specific logic.
- Each trigger type has its own configuration, payload structure, and required callback signature.
- Summarized purposes: Cron Trigger runs workflows on a time-based schedule, and the HTTP Trigger starts workflows in response to an HTTP request from an external system.

results.prompt: I'm new to Chainlink CRE and I want to kick off one of my workflows whenever an outside system sends a web request to it. How would I set that up and what is that kind of trigger called?

## The trigger is called an "HTTP Trigger"

In Chainlink CRE, the mechanism for kicking off a workflow when an outside system sends a web request is the **HTTP Trigger**. The Chainlink documentation covers the HTTP Trigger with pages dedicated to its configuration and handler, and there's a dedicated HTTP Trigger Overview as well as an SDK Reference for the HTTP Trigger.

It falls under the broader **Trigger Capability** — the trigger capability is what allows workflows to be initiated, and CRE supports several trigger types (HTTP, cron/time-based, and on-chain event triggers) documented under the "Using Triggers" section.

## How to set it up (general approach)

While I wasn't able to pull the full step-by-step details from the docs (I hit a search rate limit), here's the general shape of what an HTTP-triggered CRE workflow setup involves, and where to look:

1. **Register the HTTP trigger in your workflow** — In your workflow code, you subscribe to/register an HTTP trigger and attach a handler function that runs whenever a request comes in.

2. **Configure the trigger** — This is where you define authorization (which callers/keys are allowed to invoke the workflow), input schema, and any rate/config settings. See the **HTTP Trigger: Configuration & Handler** page: `https://docs.chain.link/cre/guides/workflow/using-triggers/http-trigger/configuration-go`

3. **Implement the handler** — Your handler receives the incoming request payload and executes your workflow logic in response.

4. **Deploy the workflow** — Once deployed to the CRE, external systems can send requests to invoke it.

## Recommended docs to read (in order)

- **HTTP Trigger Overview** — `https://docs.chain.link/cre/guides/workflow/using-triggers/http-trigger/overview-go` (start here for the concept)
- **HTTP Trigger: Configuration & Handler** — `https://docs.chain.link/cre/guides/workflow/using-triggers/http-trigger/configuration-go` (the practical setup)
- **SDK Reference: HTTP Trigger** — `https://docs.chain.link/cre/reference/sdk/triggers/http-trigger-go` (API-level details)
- **Using Triggers (overview)** — `https://docs.chain.link/cre/guides/workflow/using-triggers/overview` (to compare against other trigger types)

One note as you get started: the docs have both Go and TypeScript variants (the `-go` / `-ts` suffixes in the URLs), so pick the SDK reference matching your language.
